# Working remotely {#sec-working-remotely}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Log in to a cluster with an SSH key protected by a passphrase (or
   your site's certificate), and explain what the public and private
   halves are for and which one never leaves your laptop.
2. Write `~/.ssh/config` entries that give hosts short names, keep
   connections alive, and share one sign-in across connections, check
   them with `ssh -G`, and recognise a jump-host (`ProxyJump`) entry.
3. Start, detach from, and reattach to a tmux session, so work survives
   a dropped connection, and find the login node it lives on.
4. Copy files and folders between laptop and cluster through the data
   transfer node with `rsync` and `scp`, keeping files in the
   project's group, and choose Globus for large or many files.
5. Prove that a transfer arrived intact with `md5sum -c` on the
   receiving machine, and move the project (files, environment,
   reference link) so its pipeline runs on the cluster.
:::

## What this chapter does {#sec-working-remotely-intro}

In @sec-book-setup-ssh you logged in to a cluster once, typed
`hostname`, and logged out. Daily work is different: many logins a day,
commands that run longer than your connection lasts, and files moving
both ways. This chapter makes those three things routine. Everything
before it ran on your laptop (@sec-orientation); from here on, the main
path **assumes a cluster account**. If you do not have one yet, every
section says which steps work on the laptop alone, and the cluster
steps are shown as captured sessions you can read.

Three machines matter from now on (@fig-three-machines):

- your **laptop**, where you type `ssh`, `rsync`, and `scp`;
- the cluster's **login node**, where you log in, edit, and submit work;
- the cluster's **data transfer node (DTN)**, where files go in and out.

The login node and the DTN sit on the same shared storage, so a file
copied to the DTN appears in the same `/work` or `/project` folder you
see from the login node. We start every transfer **from the laptop**,
in both directions: a laptop behind a home or campus firewall usually
cannot accept an incoming SSH connection, so the cluster cannot start
a copy to it. Who starts the connection is separate from which way the
data flows. A "pull" typed on the laptop still moves files from the
cluster to the laptop.

::: {#fig-three-machines}
{{< svg ../figures/three-machines.svg >}}

The three machines of this chapter. You type `ssh` on the laptop to
reach the login node, and `rsync` or `scp` to reach the data transfer
node (DTN). The laptop starts every connection; files then flow in
either direction. The login node and the DTN share the cluster's
storage, so files sent to the DTN appear in your folder on the login
node. Jobs on compute nodes are @sec-hpc-slurm.
:::

Practice happens in a scratch folder on the laptop. Make it now:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch09 && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch09
```

The cluster steps use your own cluster folder: `/work/<group>/<netid>`
on Nova, `/project/<project>/<you>` on SCINet. What those storage
areas are, and why this is the right place, comes in @sec-hpc-slurm.
Two things outside the scratch folder change: your `~/.ssh` folder
(keys and config, in @sec-working-remotely-keys and
@sec-working-remotely-config) and, at the end, a copy of your project
on the cluster.

**Two laptop tools.** This chapter needs a current `rsync` and `tmux`
on the laptop. A Mac's own `/usr/bin/rsync` is an older replacement
(openrsync, "rsync version 2.6.9 compatible") that lacks options used
here, and macOS has no tmux. Install both with Homebrew, then check
that Homebrew's rsync comes first on your `PATH` (@sec-linux-system-path):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop, macOS)"}
brew install rsync tmux
type -a rsync
rsync --version | head -n 1
```

```{.console}
rsync is /usr/local/bin/rsync
rsync is /usr/bin/rsync
rsync  version 3.5.0  protocol version 32
```

(On an Apple-silicon Mac the first path is `/opt/homebrew/bin/rsync`.)
Ubuntu, including Ubuntu under WSL, already has both: Ubuntu 26.04
ships rsync 3.4.1, tmux 3.6, screen, and OpenSSH 10.2. If `type -a
rsync` or `type -a tmux` finds nothing on your Linux machine, `sudo apt
install rsync tmux` adds them.

**Without a cluster**, these parts work on the laptop alone: the
broken-transfer demonstration in @sec-working-remotely-command, making
a key in @sec-working-remotely-keys, checking a config file with `ssh
-G` in @sec-working-remotely-config, all of tmux on the laptop in
@sec-working-remotely-tmux, and the local `rsync` and checksum steps in
@sec-working-remotely-transfer and @sec-working-remotely-move.

The outputs shown were captured in November 2026: on a Mac (macOS 15,
Homebrew bash, rsync 3.5.0, OpenSSH 9.9, tmux 3.7), on Windows 11 with
Ubuntu 26.04 under WSL (OpenSSH 10.2), and by logging in to Nova,
Atlas, and Ceres. User names, groups, and addresses are replaced by
placeholders such as `<netid>`, `<group>`, and `<project>`.

## One command on another machine {#sec-working-remotely-command}

You do not have to log in to run something on the cluster. Give `ssh` a
command after the host name, and it logs in, runs that command, prints
its output on your laptop, and logs out. From the laptop, using the
short name `nova` you set up in @sec-book-setup-ssh (SCINet readers
use `ceres.scinet.usda.gov` or `atlas-login.hpc.msstate.edu`):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh nova hostname
ssh nova 'pwd; ls'
```

```{.console}
nova-login-2
/home/<netid>
…
```

(the `…` is the list of files in your cluster home). There was no prompt on the cluster and no `exit`: the command ran on
the login node and the connection closed when it finished. This is the
`ssh host command` row of @tbl-startup-files: bash on the cluster
starts without your interactive settings, runs the command, and quits.

**Quotes decide where expansion happens.** The laptop's shell reads
your command line first, then `ssh` sends what is left to the cluster.
In double quotes, the laptop expands `$HOME` before `ssh` ever runs; in
single quotes, the text travels unchanged and the cluster's shell
expands it (@sec-shell-basics):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh nova "echo double: $HOME"
ssh nova 'echo single: $HOME'
ssh nova 'exit 3'; echo "status $?"
```

```{.console}
double: /Users/you
single: /home/<netid>
status 3
```

The last line shows that the remote command's exit status comes back to
your laptop, so `&&` and `if` (@sec-shell-scripts-conditionals) work
across the connection too.

**Why this matters for copying files.** `ssh host command` is exactly
how `rsync` works: it runs `rsync` on the cluster through `ssh` and the
two copies talk to each other over the connection, byte by byte. If the
cluster's shell prints anything on standard output while it starts, a
welcome line from `~/.bashrc`, say, that text lands in the middle of
rsync's conversation and corrupts it. @sec-linux-system-startup warned
that nothing in `~/.bashrc` should print; here is what happens when
something does.

You can see it without a cluster. Make a stand-in for `ssh` that prints
one welcome line and then runs the command on your own laptop, and a
quiet version that does not print:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch09
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' \
  '# fakessh: stands in for ssh in a local demo. rsync runs it as' \
  '#   fakessh HOST COMMAND ...; it skips HOST and runs COMMAND here.' \
  'echo "Welcome to the cluster!"   # what a chatty startup file does' \
  'shift' 'exec "$@"' > fakessh
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' '# quietssh: the same, without the welcome line.' \
  'shift' 'exec "$@"' > quietssh
chmod u+x fakessh quietssh
mkdir -p src/sub && printf 'A\n' > src/a.txt && printf 'B\n' > src/sub/b.txt
```

The last line makes a small folder, `src/`, with two files; you will use
it again later. `rsync -e` names the program rsync uses instead of
`ssh`, and `localhost:` makes rsync treat the destination as "remote":

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rsync -av -e ./fakessh src/ localhost:dst-fake/; echo "exit $?"
rsync -av -e ./quietssh src/ localhost:dst-fake/; echo "exit $?"
```

```{.console}
protocol version mismatch -- is your shell clean?
(see the rsync manpage for an explanation)
rsync error: protocol incompatibility (code 2) at compat.c(625) [sender=3.5.0]
exit 2
sending incremental file list
created directory dst-fake
./
a.txt
sub/
sub/b.txt

sent 234 bytes  received 100 bytes  222.67 bytes/sec
total size is 4  speedup is 0.01
exit 0
```

The one welcome line broke the transfer; without it, the same copy
worked. rsync's own message, "is your shell clean?", is the clue to
remember. (Current versions of `scp` copy over a different channel,
SFTP, and are less sensitive; older `scp` broke the same way.)

Test your real cluster the same way. `wc -c` counts the bytes that came
back; `PIPESTATUS[0]` (@sec-shell-scripts-strict) is the exit status of
`ssh` itself, because zero bytes from a connection that failed prove
nothing:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh nova true | wc -c; echo "ssh status ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
```

```{.console}
0
ssh status 0
```

`0` and status `0` mean a clean shell. This was the result on Nova,
Atlas, and Ceres, even with a heavily customised `~/.bashrc` on Nova.
Atlas prints a long legal notice on every connection, but on standard
error, which goes to your screen and not into the pipe, so it is
harmless. If you see a number above 0, look for an `echo` or other
output in your cluster startup files (@sec-linux-system-startup);
occasionally a site's own login scripts print, and then the site has to
fix it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: a startup file that prints breaks file transfers
Text printed on standard output when the remote shell starts breaks
`rsync` (and older `scp`) with "protocol version mismatch -- is your
shell clean?". `ssh host true | wc -c` must print `0`, with ssh's own
exit status 0.
:::

**The host key, again.** In @sec-book-setup-ssh you answered `yes` to
a host-key question, and ssh saved the machine's key in
`~/.ssh/known_hosts`. Every later login checks that key. If it ever
differs, ssh stops with a warning you should never ignore. Here it is,
made safely by pointing ssh at a fake `known_hosts` file:

```{.console}
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
@    WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!     @
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY!
Someone could be eavesdropping on you right now (man-in-the-middle attack)!
It is also possible that a host key has just been changed.
The fingerprint for the ED25519 key sent by the remote host is
SHA256:DRxKEui9nnf4BSBeLSN4mZ5Il3eHjsoiN74EvzSlmxE.
Please contact your system administrator.
Add correct host key in ./fake_known_hosts to get rid of this message.
Offending ED25519 key in ./fake_known_hosts:1
Host key for nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu has changed and you have requested strict checking.
Host key verification failed.
```

ssh refused to connect (exit status 255). There are two possible
reasons: the site really changed its keys, which sites announce (check
its news, or its published fingerprints, such as [Nova's
list](https://research.it.iastate.edu/nova-ssh-host-key-fingerprints)),
or something between you and the cluster is pretending to be it. Do not
"fix" the warning by deleting `known_hosts`. Once the site confirms a
change, remove that one entry and connect again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh-keygen -R nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu
```

A **harmless** cousin of this message appears the first time you use a
new name for a machine you already know, such as `nova-login-1` after
`nova`:

```{.console}
The authenticity of host 'nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu (10.94.0.3)' can't be established.
ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:DRxKEui9nnf4BSBeLSN4mZ5Il3eHjsoiN74EvzSlmxE.
This host key is known by the following other names/addresses:
    ~/.ssh/known_hosts:8: nova.its.iastate.edu
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])?
```

This is the ordinary question, and ssh even tells you it has seen this
key under another name: all of Nova's login names share one key. Type
`yes`.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `ssh nova "echo $USER"` and `ssh nova 'echo
$USER'` print different names on a laptop where your user name differs
from your cluster name. Which one is the cluster's?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The single-quoted one. In double quotes, the laptop's shell replaces
`$USER` with your laptop user name before `ssh` sends the command; in
single quotes, `$USER` travels to the cluster and its shell expands it.
:::
:::

## SSH keys: logging in without retyping a password {#sec-working-remotely-keys}

Typing a code and a password for every connection gets tiring fast, and
on Nova it is worse than it sounds: an authenticator code cannot be
used twice, so two connections in the same 30 seconds fail on the
second and ask again. An **SSH key** replaces both with something you
hold.

**Make a key** (laptop; no cluster needed):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "laptop-2026"
```

`-t ed25519` picks the key type (the modern, short, recommended one);
`-C` adds a comment, a label so you can tell your keys apart later. Press
{{< kbd Enter >}} to accept the suggested file, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`.
**If it asks `Overwrite (y/n)?`, answer `n`**: you already have a key
with that name, and overwriting it would lock you out of everywhere it
is installed. Then **set a passphrase**: a phrase you will remember,
typed twice. Nothing appears as you type.

```{.console}
Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Enter file in which to save the key (/home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519):
Enter passphrase for "/home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519" (empty for no passphrase):
Enter same passphrase again:
Your identification has been saved in /home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519
Your public key has been saved in /home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:/s+YthFDm8UJK3tgWIr5BkzCct90X9txEF/qLboNueA laptop-2026
The key's randomart image is:
+--[ED25519 256]--+
…
+----[SHA256]-----+
```

That is OpenSSH 10's wording; older versions ask `Enter passphrase
(empty for no passphrase):`. If the two passphrases differ, it says
`Passphrases do not match.  Try again.` and asks again. (The key shown
throughout this chapter is a throwaway made for the book.)

Look at what you made:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls -l ~/.ssh/id_ed25519*
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

```{.console}
-rw------- 1 you you 464 Nov 23 10:16 /home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you  96 Nov 23 10:16 /home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAA… laptop-2026
256 SHA256:/s+YthFDm8UJK3tgWIr5BkzCct90X9txEF/qLboNueA laptop-2026 (ED25519)
```

A key is **two files** (@fig-ssh-key-login):

- the **public key**, `id_ed25519.pub`: one line, safe to share. You
  give a copy to every machine you want to log in to, which keeps it in
  a list called `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`;
- the **private key**, `id_ed25519` (no `.pub`): it stays on your
  laptop. At login, the server sends a challenge, your laptop signs it
  with the private key, and the server checks the signature with the
  public key. The private key itself is never sent.

The **passphrase** encrypts the private key on disk, so a copy of the
file is useless without it.

::: {#fig-ssh-key-login}
{{< svg ../figures/ssh-key-login.svg >}}

How key login works. `ssh-keygen` makes a pair of keys on your laptop;
the public key is copied once to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the
cluster; at each login the server sends a challenge, the laptop signs it
with the private key, and the server checks the signature with the
public key. The private key never crosses to the cluster.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
The public key is a lock you can give to any machine; the private key
is the only key that fits it, and it stays on your laptop, protected by
a passphrase.
:::

**Permissions.** ssh refuses a private key that others could read
(@tbl-chmod-recipes: `~/.ssh` at `700`, the private key at `600`;
`ssh-keygen` sets both). If a copy goes wrong, you will see:

```{.console}
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
@         WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!          @
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
Permissions 0644 for 'id_ed25519' are too open.
It is required that your private key files are NOT accessible by others.
This private key will be ignored.
Load key "id_ed25519": bad permissions
```

`chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` fixes it.

**Type the passphrase once: the agent.** An **ssh-agent** is a small
program that holds your unlocked key in memory, so you type the
passphrase once per session instead of at every login. `ssh-add` hands
it a key, and `ssh-add -l` lists the keys it holds.

- **macOS** runs an agent for you. Add these lines at the **end** of
  `~/.ssh/config` (@sec-working-remotely-config explains the file):

  ```{.default filename="~/.ssh/config (laptop, macOS)"}
  Host *
      AddKeysToAgent yes
      UseKeychain yes
  ```

  The first login then asks for the passphrase once, loads the key
  into the agent, and saves the passphrase in your Keychain; after that,
  logins ask nothing, even after a restart. You do not need `ssh-add`.
  (`UseKeychain` exists only in Apple's ssh.)
- **Ubuntu under WSL** has no agent in a new terminal. Start one, then
  add your key:

  ```{.bash filename="Terminal (Ubuntu)"}
  echo "SSH_AUTH_SOCK=[$SSH_AUTH_SOCK]"
  ssh-add -l
  eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
  ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  ssh-add -l
  ```

  ```{.console}
  SSH_AUTH_SOCK=[]
  Could not open a connection to your authentication agent.
  Agent pid 649
  Enter passphrase for /home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519:
  Identity added: /home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519 (laptop-2026)
  256 SHA256:/s+YthFDm8UJK3tgWIr5BkzCct90X9txEF/qLboNueA laptop-2026 (ED25519)
  ```

  This terminal now knows how to reach the agent; a new terminal
  normally does not, so you repeat these lines there. The agent itself
  runs in the background and can keep running after you close the
  terminal, so before you close it, stop the agent you started:

  ```{.bash filename="Terminal (Ubuntu)"}
  eval "$(ssh-agent -k)"
  ```

  (This is only for an agent you started by hand like this; the Mac's
  own agent needs nothing. OpenSSH 10 keeps the agent's connection
  point in `~/.ssh/agent/`, so starting the agent creates `~/.ssh` if
  you did not have one yet.)

**Install the public key, by site.** How a cluster learns your public
key depends on the site, so check its page first (@tbl-site-login).

- **Nova.** ISU allows key login as an alternative to the
  authenticator code: "Public key authentication does not use TOTP
  keys" ([ISU: login to Nova with an SSH
  client](https://research.it.iastate.edu/login-nova-ssh-client)). Keys
  work only over the **ISU VPN**, "regardless of whether you are on or
  off campus", and go to a **named** login node, because
  `nova.its.iastate.edu` "is not a single server". Connect the VPN,
  then send your public key with one last code-and-password login:

  ```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
  ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub <netid>@nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu
  ```

  ```{.console}
  /usr/bin/ssh-copy-id: INFO: Source of key(s) to be installed: "/home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub"
  /usr/bin/ssh-copy-id: INFO: attempting to log in with the new key(s), to filter out any that are already installed
  /usr/bin/ssh-copy-id: INFO: 1 key(s) remain to be installed -- if you are prompted now it is to install the new keys
  (<netid>@nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu) Verification code:
  (<netid>@nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu) Password:

  Number of key(s) added:        1
  ```

  `ssh-copy-id` adds your public key to the end of `authorized_keys`
  on Nova and leaves anything already there alone. Try it:

  ```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
  ssh <netid>@nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu hostname
  ```

  ```{.console}
  Enter passphrase for key '/home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519':
  nova-login-1
  ```

  The key's passphrase, and nothing else: no code, no ISU password.
  With the agent holding the key, not even that. The same key also
  works on `nova-login-2` and on the transfer node, `novadtn`.
- **SCINet.** Use SCINet's certificate route from @sec-book-setup-ssh
  and skip `ssh-copy-id`: SCINet's [SSH
  page](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/access/ssh-login) documents the
  SmallStep `step` setup, not personal keys in `authorized_keys`. A
  **certificate** is your public key plus your identity, signed by
  SCINet for the day after you sign in through the browser ("once for
  the day (or every 16 hours)"). The matching private key still stays on
  your laptop and still does the proving. Read this section for the
  idea; you will use the same kind of key for GitHub in @sec-github.
- **Other sites.** Many allow keys; some forbid them, and some require a
  second factor as well. The site's own page is the authority
  (@sec-cluster-sites).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: never share the private key
Never copy, email, paste, or upload `id_ed25519` (the file **without**
`.pub`): not to a cluster, not to a USB stick, not into a chat or an
issue. If it leaks, make a new pair and remove the old public key from
every `authorized_keys` where you installed it.
:::

**Windows: two SSH programs.** On Windows, the Ubuntu terminal and
Windows' own ssh (the one VS Code's Remote-SSH uses,
@sec-book-setup-remote) are separate programs with separate `~/.ssh`
folders. Each one needs its own setup:

- **Keys (Nova):** make one key pair in the Ubuntu terminal and another
  in PowerShell (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "windows-2026"`), and install
  both public keys. Do not share one private key between the two.
- **SCINet:** `step` sets up only the ssh program it is run from, so a
  setup in Ubuntu does nothing for VS Code on Windows. Windows' `step`
  also needs the Windows `ssh-agent` service running ("If it is not
  running, SmallStepCLI will not work", says SCINet's page), and on a
  standard Windows 11 that service is `Stopped` and `Disabled`, which
  only an administrator can change. Unless you have admin rights, use
  Open OnDemand for VS Code on SCINet (@sec-book-setup-remote).

A Windows home folder can contain a space (`C:\Users\Jane Doe`). Paths
under it must be quoted in ssh options, or ssh reads the second half as
an extra word ("extra arguments at end of line").

: How you prove who you are at the two example sites. Observed
2026-11-22/23; your site's own pages are the authority
(@sec-cluster-sites). {#tbl-site-login}

| | Nova (Iowa State) | SCINet (Ceres, Atlas) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Sign-in without a key | authenticator code, then password, for every connection | a browser sign-in about once a day (`step`) |
| Keys | allowed, over the ISU VPN; `ssh-copy-id` to `nova-login-1` or `-2` | not documented; use the `step` certificate |
| What a login asks once set up | the key's passphrase once, then nothing (agent) | nothing until the certificate expires |
| Windows | one key in Ubuntu, another in PowerShell | `step` in each ssh program; Windows needs the `ssh-agent` service (admin), or use Open OnDemand |
| Quick connections in a row | a code cannot be reused, so expect to wait for a new code without a key | no effect |

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "My public key is the secret one, and the private key is what I give to servers"
**Reality.** It is the other way round. The public key (`.pub`) is
meant to be shared and goes on every server; the private key never
leaves your laptop.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A labmate asks for "your SSH key" so they can give
you access to a server. Which file do you send?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`, the public key. Never the file without `.pub`.
:::
:::

## `~/.ssh/config`: names, keep-alives, one sign-in, jump hosts {#sec-working-remotely-config}

In @sec-book-setup-ssh you wrote a three-line entry so that `ssh nova`
meant `ssh <netid>@nova.its.iastate.edu`. The same file can hold
everything else you would otherwise type each time. Before changing
your real one, back it up under a dated name:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp ~/.ssh/config ~/.ssh/config.bak-$(date +%F)
ls -l ~/.ssh
```

(If `cp` says there is no such file, you have no config yet; carry on.)
**No cluster account?** Do the same work in a practice file instead, so
your real config gets no made-up hosts: `code
~/bioinf-computing-ch09/sample-config`, and add `-F sample-config` to
every `ssh -G` below.

**Ask ssh what it will do.** `ssh -G host` prints the settings ssh would
use for that host, after reading your config, **without connecting**.
It is the way to check every change in this section. With the entry
from @sec-book-setup-ssh plus a second one for the transfer node:

```{.default filename="~/.ssh/config (laptop)"}
Host nova
    HostName nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu

Host nova-dtn
    HostName novadtn.its.iastate.edu

Host nova nova-dtn
    User <netid>
```

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh -G nova-dtn | grep -E '^(hostname|user|serveraliveinterval|controlmaster) '
```

```{.console}
user <netid>
hostname novadtn.its.iastate.edu
controlmaster false
serveraliveinterval 0
```

Note the first change from @sec-book-setup-ssh: `HostName` is now the
**named** login node `nova-login-1` rather than `nova.its.iastate.edu`.
Keys need a named node on Nova, and so does tmux
(@sec-working-remotely-tmux).

A `Host` line can list several names, and every block whose names match
is read. For most options, **the first value found wins**, so specific
blocks go first and shared ones after; a `Host *` block, which matches
everything, goes last (the same "first match" idea as `PATH`,
@sec-linux-system-path). Here is the book's full Nova block, one
option at a time:

```{.default filename="~/.ssh/config (laptop)"}
Host nova
    HostName nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu

Host nova-dtn
    HostName novadtn.its.iastate.edu

Host nova nova-dtn
    User <netid>
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    IdentitiesOnly yes
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
    ControlPersist 10h
```

- `IdentityFile` names your private key, and `IdentitiesOnly yes` tells
  ssh to offer **only** that one. Without it, ssh offers every key the
  agent holds (a GitHub key, a SCINet certificate, …) one after another,
  and servers give up after a few wrong ones.
- `ServerAliveInterval 60` sends a small "still here" message every 60
  seconds. It stops a firewall or VPN from dropping a connection that
  sits idle (ISU recommends it in its
  [FAQ](https://research.it.iastate.edu/faqs)). It cannot bring back a
  VPN or a network that has failed.
- `ControlMaster`, `ControlPath`, `ControlPersist`: **connection
  sharing**, below.

Check it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh -G nova-dtn | grep -E '^(user|hostname|identitiesonly|serveraliveinterval|control)'
```

```{.console}
user <netid>
hostname novadtn.its.iastate.edu
controlmaster auto
identitiesonly yes
serveraliveinterval 60
controlpath /home/you/.ssh/cm-3631c01c705606618c1a8ba73b84c46359830ac2
controlpersist 36000
```

`%C` became a long hash of your user, host, and port, and `10h` became
36,000 seconds.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tip
`ssh -G <host>` shows what ssh will do with your config, without
connecting. Run it after every change.
:::

**Connection sharing.** With `ControlMaster auto`, the first connection
to a host signs in and becomes the **master**; later connections to the
**same host** (a second terminal, an `rsync`, an `scp`) travel inside it
and sign in to nothing. ISU's FAQ recommends this for exactly "having
to authenticate so often". It matters most if you sign in with a code;
with a key in the agent, logins ask nothing anyway. On Nova, the first
`ssh nova` asked for the code and password once, a second `ssh nova`
asked nothing, and you can see the master:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh -O check nova
ssh -O check nova-dtn
ssh -O exit nova
```

```{.console}
Master running (pid=27640)
Master running (pid=28661)
Exit request sent.
```

Four details:

- It is **one master per host**. The master to `nova` does not serve
  `nova-dtn`; the transfer node needed its own sign-in, and after that,
  `rsync` and `scp` to it asked nothing. That is why the shared block
  names both.
- `ControlPersist 10h` keeps the master open for up to 10 hours **after
  the last connection using it closes**. It is an idle timeout, not a
  promise of 10 hours: the site or the network can end it sooner.
  `ssh -O exit` closes it now.
- `ControlPath` is where the master's connection point lives. Use
  `~/.ssh/cm-%C`: the longer `cm-%r@%h:%p` form found in many guides
  failed on a Mac when the path grew too long (`unix_listener: path
  "…" too long for Unix domain socket`).
- While a master is open, anyone using your laptop account can use the
  connection. Lock your screen.

**Windows: no sharing.** Windows' own OpenSSH cannot do connection
sharing. With these three lines in `C:\Users\<you>\.ssh\config`, the
connection fails:

```{.console}
getsockname failed: Not a socket
Read from remote host nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu: Unknown error
```

Put `ControlMaster`, `ControlPath`, and `ControlPersist` only in the
Ubuntu (WSL) config. The other lines work in both.

**SCINet: `step` wrote yours.** SCINet's `step` setup added an
`Include` line to your `~/.ssh/config`; do not edit what it points to.
It is worth reading once:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
grep -n Include ~/.ssh/config
cat ~/.step/ssh/config
```

```{.console}
22:	Include "/home/you/.step/ssh/includes"
Match exec "step ssh check-host %h"
	User <first.last>
	UserKnownHostsFile "/home/you/.step/ssh/known_hosts"
	ProxyCommand step ssh proxycommand --provisioner keycloak %r %h %p
```

`Match exec` applies these settings only to hosts that `step` knows are
SCINet's. `User` is why you never type your SCINet user name.
`UserKnownHostsFile` keeps SCINet's host keys in step's own file, which
trusts any host certificate SCINet signs; that is why SCINet's login
nodes never ask the host-key question. `ProxyCommand` runs every SCINet
connection through `step`, which opens the browser for a new
certificate when the old one has expired. Two visible side effects:
connections to `atlas-dtn` print `Certificate invalid: name is not a
listed principal` and ask one ordinary host-key question, because that
node's certificate does not list the shared name. It is harmless.

If you want short names on SCINet, add your own entries **before** the
two lines `step` wrote, `Host *` and the `Include` under it. Keep those
two lines together: `Include` reads its file only for the hosts named
by the `Host` line above it, so an alias slipped in between them would
leave your other aliases without SCINet's user name, host keys, and
`step`. The end of the file should look like this (keep the `Include`
path your setup wrote):

```{.default filename="~/.ssh/config (laptop)"}
Host atlas
    HostName atlas-login.hpc.msstate.edu

Host atlas-dtn
    HostName atlas-dtn.hpc.msstate.edu

Host ceres
    HostName ceres.scinet.usda.gov

Host ceres-dtn
    HostName ceres-dtn.scinet.usda.gov

# Keep the block step wrote after your aliases.
Host *
	Include "/home/you/.step/ssh/includes"
```

Check a login alias and a transfer alias: both should show your SCINet
user name and step's `proxycommand`.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh -G atlas | grep -E '^(user|hostname|userknownhostsfile|proxycommand) '
ssh -G atlas-dtn | grep -E '^(user|hostname|userknownhostsfile|proxycommand) '
```

The rest of this chapter uses `atlas-dtn` and `ceres-dtn` only in that
sense: short names you defined.

**Jump hosts: recognising `ProxyJump`.** Some machines can be reached
only through another one: a compute node only through the login node, a
cluster only through a gateway (@fig-proxyjump). `ProxyJump` tells ssh
to go through the first machine to reach the second:

```{.default filename="~/.ssh/config (laptop)"}
Host <allocated-node>
    ProxyJump nova
```

or, once, `ssh -J nova <allocated-node>`. The placeholder must be a
compute node **you currently hold** (@sec-hpc-slurm teaches how to get
one, connect to it this way, and give it back), so there is nothing to
run yet; recognise the entry when you see it. ISU's own recipe for
editors on compute nodes adds `ForwardAgent yes` and
`StrictHostKeyChecking no` to that one entry; those are ISU's choices,
explained in @sec-hpc-slurm, and do not belong in a `Host *` block. On
Windows, a jump-host entry must be in the Windows config for VS Code to
use it.

::: {#fig-proxyjump}
{{< svg ../figures/proxyjump.svg >}}

A jump host. Your laptop cannot reach a compute node directly; with
`ProxyJump nova`, ssh connects to the login node first and goes on from
there to a node you hold. @sec-hpc-slurm shows the whole route, from
holding a node to giving it back.
:::

: The `~/.ssh/config` options in this chapter. Full list:
[`ssh_config(5)`](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config.5). {#tbl-ssh-config-options}

| Option | What it does | Example |
|:-------|:-------------|:--------|
| `Host` | starts a block; the names you type | `Host nova nova-dtn` |
| `HostName` | the real machine behind the name | `nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu` |
| `User` | your user name there | `<netid>` |
| `IdentityFile` | which private key to use | `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` |
| `IdentitiesOnly` | offer only that key | `yes` |
| `ServerAliveInterval` | keep an idle connection open | `60` |
| `ControlMaster`, `ControlPath`, `ControlPersist` | share one sign-in per host (not in Windows' own ssh) | `auto`, `~/.ssh/cm-%C`, `10h` |
| `ProxyJump` | go through another host first | `nova` (@sec-hpc-slurm) |
| `AddKeysToAgent`, `UseKeychain` | load the key and remember its passphrase (macOS) | `yes` |
| `Include` | read another config file | written by `step` on SCINet |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Your config has `Host *` with `User guest` at the
top, and `Host nova` with `User <netid>` below it. Which user does `ssh
nova` use, and how do you check?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`guest`: for most options the first value found wins, and `Host *`
matches first. `ssh -G nova | grep '^user '` shows it without
connecting. Move the `Host *` block to the end.
:::
:::

## tmux: work that survives a dropped connection {#sec-working-remotely-tmux}

Close your laptop, lose Wi-Fi, or let the VPN time out, and an SSH
session ends, taking the commands running in it along
(@sec-linux-system-processes). **tmux** keeps a shell running on the
machine itself, so you can leave and come back to it.

Try it on the laptop first. Make a small script that prints the time
every five seconds:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch09
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' \
  '# ticker.sh: print the time every 5 seconds until stopped (Ctrl-C).' \
  'while true; do date +%T; sleep 5; done' > ticker.sh
```

Start a tmux session named `ch09`, and run the ticker inside it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tmux new -s ch09
bash ticker.sh
```

A green bar appears at the bottom: you are inside tmux. Now **detach**:
press {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}}, let go, then press {{< kbd D >}}. You are back
in your ordinary terminal, and tmux says:

```{.console}
[detached (from session ch09)]
```

Close the **whole terminal window**. Open a new one and look:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tmux ls
tmux attach -t ch09
```

```{.console}
ch09: 1 windows (created Sun Nov 22 15:30:08 2026)
```

The ticker is still running, with no gap in the times: it never
noticed that you left. Stop it with {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} and type `exit`
to end the session.

**The same on the cluster.** Log in, note where you are, and start the
ticker in tmux:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
hostname
tmux new -s ch09
```

Run the same `while true; do date +%T; sleep 5; done` line inside it
(or copy `ticker.sh` over first; @sec-working-remotely-transfer shows
how), detach, and this time **turn your Wi-Fi off for a minute**. The
frozen terminal finally gives up:

```{.console}
Connection to nova.its.iastate.edu closed by remote host.
Connection to nova.its.iastate.edu closed.
client_loop: send disconnect: Broken pipe
```

Reconnect, `tmux attach -t ch09`, and the ticker is still counting,
with no gap across the minute you were gone. This was the result on
Nova and on Atlas. The green bar even shows the node's name
(`"nova-login-1"`), a free reminder of where the session lives.

**What happened** (@fig-tmux-detach). When you start tmux, it starts a
**tmux server** on that machine, which owns the shell and everything
running in it. Your terminal is only a **client** that shows the
server's screen. A dropped connection kills the client, not the
server, so the work goes on and you can attach a new client later.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
tmux keeps the shell on the remote machine; your connection only views
it, so losing the connection loses the view, not the work.
:::

::: {#fig-tmux-detach}
{{< svg ../figures/tmux-detach.svg >}}

Why a tmux session survives, and how it seems to vanish. The tmux server
runs on the login node where you started it; your terminal is only a
client. A dropped connection ends the client, not the server. But a
cluster can have several login nodes, and a session on one is invisible
from another: reconnect to the node you started on. tmux survives
disconnects, not reboots or a site's cleanup.
:::

**Where it lives.** A tmux session exists on **one** machine. Nova has
two login nodes, and `nova.its.iastate.edu` sends each login to either
at random (ISU's FAQ says so, and repeated logins landed on `-2`, `-2`,
`-1`, `-2`). A session started on `nova-login-1` is invisible from
`nova-login-2`:

```{.console}
$ ssh <netid>@nova.its.iastate.edu 'hostname; tmux ls'
nova-login-2
error connecting to /tmp/tmux-<uid>/default (No such file or directory)
$ ssh <netid>@nova.its.iastate.edu 'hostname; tmux ls'
nova-login-1
ch09: 1 windows (created Sun Nov 22 21:17:25 2026)
```

The habit: run `hostname` before you detach, and put a named node in
your config (`HostName nova-login-1`, as in
@sec-working-remotely-config), so `ssh nova` always lands where your
session is: `ssh -t nova tmux attach -t ch09` reconnects and
reattaches in one go. To reach a node your config does not name, give
your user name too, because a full host name does not match the `Host
nova` block and ssh would use your laptop user name: `ssh -t
<netid>@nova-login-2.its.iastate.edu tmux attach -t ch09`.

On SCINet, Atlas's `atlas-login` name hands out two login nodes, and
both can be reached by name (`atlas-login-1.hpc.msstate.edu`,
`atlas-login-2.hpc.msstate.edu`) without any extra question. Ceres's
name led to `ceres-login-1`. The same habit applies everywhere.

The "nothing here" message has two forms in the tmux version on these
clusters (3.2a): `error connecting to … (No such file or directory)`
where tmux has never run, and `no server running on …` where a session
used to be. Newer versions say `no server running on …`. Both mean no
session on **this** machine.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: a session on the other login node seems to vanish
On a cluster with several login nodes, note `hostname` before you
detach. If `tmux ls` finds nothing, check which node you are on before
assuming the session is gone.
:::

**What tmux does not do.** tmux on a login node is still the login node:
fine for editing, short commands, and watching something small, but
heavy work belongs in a job (@sec-hpc-slurm), which keeps running
without tmux, or you. A session also ends when its server ends: when
the node reboots (Nova's login banner announces its next maintenance
date), when you kill it, or when the site cleans up old processes. And
transfers from your laptop are not login-node work at all: they run on
the laptop (@sec-working-remotely-transfer). tmux on the **laptop**
protects a transfer's terminal from a closed window, not from the laptop
going to sleep, and nothing can copy from a laptop that is asleep.
Globus helps in other ways (@sec-working-remotely-transfer): it carries
on with a cluster-to-cluster transfer however your laptop is, and it
resumes a laptop transfer when the laptop is back online.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "If I close the window, the command stops; if I keep it open, it runs"
**Reality.** A command in an ordinary SSH session usually stops when the
connection drops, whether you closed the window or the network failed.
Inside tmux, it keeps running on the remote machine whatever happens to
your window, until the session itself ends. For long work, use tmux, or
better, a scheduler job.
:::

**A handful of keys.** Every tmux shortcut starts with {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}}
(press, let go, then the key). Scrolling is the one that surprises
people: the mouse wheel does **not** scroll tmux by default. In iTerm2
and similar terminals it sends arrow keys instead, which step through
your command history at a prompt, or type `^[[A^[[B…` into a running
program. Use {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd [ >}}, then the arrow keys or
Page Up, and {{< kbd q >}} to leave.

: tmux in eight commands, with GNU `screen`, an older program that does
the same, beside it. {#tbl-tmux-keys}

| Task | tmux | screen |
|:-----|:-----|:-------|
| New named session | `tmux new -s name` | `screen -S name` |
| Detach | {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd D >}} | {{< kbd Ctrl-A >}} {{< kbd D >}} |
| List sessions | `tmux ls` | `screen -ls` |
| Attach | `tmux attach -t name` | `screen -r name` |
| End a session | `exit` inside it, or `tmux kill-session -t name` | `exit` inside it |
| Scroll back | {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd [ >}}, arrows, {{< kbd q >}} | {{< kbd Ctrl-A >}} {{< kbd Esc >}}, arrows, {{< kbd Esc >}} |
| New window, next window | {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd C >}}, {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd N >}} | {{< kbd Ctrl-A >}} {{< kbd C >}}, {{< kbd Ctrl-A >}} {{< kbd N >}} |
| Split the screen | {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd % >}} (side by side) | {{< kbd Ctrl-A >}} {{< kbd S >}} (top and bottom) |
| On our clusters | Nova, Atlas, Ceres (3.2a; Atlas and Ceres also have newer versions as modules) | Ceres only |

Use whichever your site has; the idea is the same.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You detached from tmux on Nova yesterday; today
`tmux ls` says `no server running` (or `error connecting to …`). Give
two possible reasons.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
You landed on the other login node, or the session ended (the node
rebooted, or the site cleaned it up). Check `hostname`, and try the
other node by name.
:::
:::

## Moving files: `rsync`, `scp`, and the DTN {#sec-working-remotely-transfer}

`rsync` copies files and folders, locally or between machines, and
sends only what changed. Learn it on the laptop, where mistakes cost
nothing, using the `src/` folder from @sec-working-remotely-command.
Delete the demo copy first:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch09
rm -r dst-fake
find src | sort
```

```{.console}
src
src/a.txt
src/sub
src/sub/b.txt
```

**Dry run first.** `-n` (or `--dry-run`) shows what rsync would do and
does nothing:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rsync -av --dry-run src/ dst3
```

```{.console}
sending incremental file list
created directory dst3
./
a.txt
sub/
sub/b.txt

sent 142 bytes  received 56 bytes  396.00 bytes/sec
total size is 4  speedup is 0.02 (DRY RUN)
```

`(DRY RUN)` at the end, and `dst3` still does not exist. `-a`
("archive") copies folders and keeps times, permissions, and links; `-v`
lists each file. Now copy for real, then add a file and copy again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rsync -av src/ dst3
printf 'C\n' > src/c.txt
rsync -av src/ dst3
```

```{.console}
sending incremental file list
created directory dst3
./
a.txt
sub/
sub/b.txt

sent 234 bytes  received 96 bytes  660.00 bytes/sec
total size is 4  speedup is 0.01
sending incremental file list
./
c.txt

sent 206 bytes  received 39 bytes  490.00 bytes/sec
total size is 6  speedup is 0.02
```

The second run sent only `c.txt`. rsync compares the two sides and
skips files that already match, so rerunning a large copy after an
interruption costs little.

**The trailing slash.** Whether the source ends in `/` changes what
arrives (@fig-rsync-slash):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rsync -a src dst1
rsync -a src/ dst2
find dst1 dst2 | sort
```

```{.console}
dst1
dst1/src
dst1/src/a.txt
dst1/src/c.txt
dst1/src/sub
dst1/src/sub/b.txt
dst2
dst2/a.txt
dst2/c.txt
dst2/sub
dst2/sub/b.txt
```

Without the slash, rsync copies the folder `src` itself into `dst1`;
with it, it copies what is **inside** `src`. A slash on the destination
makes no difference (`dst2` and `dst2/` give the same result).

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
A slash at the end of the source means "the contents of": `rsync -a
src/ dst` puts the files in `dst`; `rsync -a src dst` puts a folder
`src` in `dst`.
:::

::: {#fig-rsync-slash}
{{< svg ../figures/rsync-slash.svg >}}

The trailing slash on the source. `rsync -a src dst1` copies the folder
itself, so the files end up in `dst1/src/`; `rsync -a src/ dst2` copies
its contents, so they end up directly in `dst2/`. Below: a second run
sends only what changed, here the new file `c.txt`.
:::

**To and from the cluster.** The same command works between machines:
put `host:path` on one side. Type it **on the laptop**, and send it to
the **transfer node**, never the login node (@sec-book-setup-ssh). Upload
raw data, download results:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rsync -av --no-p --no-g data/ nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/myproject/data/
rsync -av nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/myproject/results/ results/
```

Three rules make this reliable.

**1. Make the destination first.** rsync creates only the **last**
folder of a destination path, not missing folders above it:

```{.console}
$ rsync -av src/ nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/missing/a/b/
sending incremental file list
rsync: [Receiver] mkdir "/work/<group>/<netid>/missing/a/b" failed: No such file or directory (2)
rsync error: error in file IO (code 11) at main.c(780) [Receiver=3.2.5]
```

Make the folder on the cluster first, with `mkdir -p` sent through
`ssh` (the login node and the DTN see the same storage, so either
works): `ssh nova 'mkdir -p /work/<group>/<netid>/myproject/data'`.
Newer rsyncs have a `--mkpath` option for this; the clusters have it,
but older laptops do not, so this book does not rely on it.

**2. Into a project folder, add `--no-p --no-g`.** Project folders are
**group folders**: everything in them should belong to the project's
group, so your labmates can use it. They are set up so that new files
inherit that group (the `s` in `drwxrws---`, the setgid bit of
@sec-linux-system-permissions). Plain `-a` gets in the way, because it
copies the laptop's group and permission bits. On all three clusters,
files copied with plain `-av` ended up in your **personal** group
instead of the project's, and on Nova the folder also lost its `s`.
`--no-p` (do not copy permission bits) and `--no-g` (do not copy the
group) let the cluster's own rules decide: the files get the project's
group and the site's default permissions. This is SCINet's own
recommendation ([SCINet: local data
transfer](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/data/transfer/local)), which
also adds `-z` (compress on the way):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rsync -avz --no-p --no-g data/ atlas-dtn:/project/<project>/<you>/myproject/data/
```

Files that are read-only on your laptop, like your `data/raw` from
@sec-organizing-projects-raw, still arrive read-only. Use plain `-a`
for copies on your laptop and for downloads to it.

**3. Rerun to finish, `-P` for big files.** If a transfer stops, run the
same command again: rsync skips what already arrived. For large files,
`-P` shows progress and keeps a partly sent file, so the rerun resumes
it instead of starting over. On Atlas and Ceres, a second run with
`--no-p --no-g` sends nothing. Through Nova's `novadtn`, files copied
this way currently get the time of the copy instead of the laptop's,
so every rerun checks every file again; the result is still correct,
only slower (observed November 2026; reported to ISU).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: rsync does not make missing parent folders
`rsync … host:/a/b/c/` fails with `mkdir … failed: No such file or
directory` and code 11 when `/a/b` does not exist. Make the
destination with `ssh host 'mkdir -p …'` first.
:::

You will see `rsync --delete` in other guides. It makes the destination
an exact copy by **deleting** files that are not in the source, and with
a missing slash or the two paths swapped it deletes real data. This
book does not use it; if you ever do, dry-run (`-n`) first and read
every line it lists.

**`scp` for one file.** `scp` copies single files, with the same
`host:path` form:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
scp data/raw/checksums.md5 nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/
```

It is fine for a quick file. It does not skip what is already there or
resume, and SCINet advises against `scp -r` for folders into
`/project`, because the copies do not inherit the project's group. Use
rsync for folders. @tbl-transfer-tools compares the options.

**Why the DTN.** The login node is shared by everyone logged in; a big
copy through it slows them all. The DTN is a machine built for moving
data, on the same storage, so the files land in the same `/work` or
`/project` folder. Your first connection to a DTN asks the host-key
question: it is a different machine. If a transfer fails right after
signing in with `connection unexpectedly closed` and code 255, rerun
it once; if it keeps happening, tell the site. (In November 2026, one
of Atlas's two transfer nodes did exactly that, and SCINet was told.)

**Globus, for big or many files.** For hundreds of gigabytes, thousands
of files, or a copy from one cluster to another (Ceres to Atlas, say),
use the site's **Globus** collection in a web browser: "SCINet-Ceres",
"SCINet-Atlas", or "SCINet-Juno"; "Nova DTN" at ISU
([Globus documentation](https://docs.globus.org/), [SCINet: Globus
data transfer](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/data/transfer/globus)).
You pick the two ends and the folders in a web page; Globus runs the
transfer on its own, restarts it after failures, and can email you when
it is done. You can close the browser. A transfer between two clusters
needs no laptop at all, so it carries on while your laptop sleeps.
Globus Connect Personal makes your laptop one end; then the files move
directly from (or to) the laptop, so keep it awake and online with
Globus Connect Personal running. If it does sleep, Globus resumes when
it is back. Small files on SCINet can also go through Open
OnDemand's file manager (SCINet suggests it for less than 1 GB). The
recipes are in @sec-cluster-sites-transfer.

: Ways to move files between your laptop and a cluster.
{#tbl-transfer-tools}

| Tool | Best for | Resumes? | Notes |
|:-----|:---------|:---------|:------|
| `rsync` | folders, repeat copies | yes (rerun; `-P` for big files) | into project folders: `-av --no-p --no-g` (SCINet adds `-z`) |
| `scp` | one quick file | no | SCINet: not `scp -r` into `/project` |
| `sftp`, Cyberduck | browsing, a few files | partly | graphical on the laptop |
| FileZilla | a few files | partly | Nova only, one connection, or it asks for the code again and again; SCINet does not support it |
| Globus | large or many files, cluster to cluster | yes, automatically | web browser; cluster to cluster runs while your laptop sleeps; a laptop end must stay awake |
| Open OnDemand file manager | small files on SCINet | no | under 1 GB |
| Rclone | cloud storage | yes | @sec-cloud |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You run `rsync -a results
nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/results`. Where do the files end up?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
In `/work/<group>/<netid>/results/results/`: without a slash on the
source, rsync copies the folder `results` into the destination folder.
Use `results/` to copy what is inside.
:::
:::

## Proving the copy, and moving the project {#sec-working-remotely-move}

A transfer that finished without an error is not yet a proven copy.
@sec-organizing-projects-raw made a checksum list for your raw data and
said to check it "after every download or transfer". Here is why, first
on the laptop. Make a checksum list in `src/`, copy, and check the copy:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch09/src && md5sum a.txt sub/b.txt > checksums.md5 && cd ..
rsync -a src/ dst3
cd dst3 && md5sum -c checksums.md5; echo "status $?"
```

```{.console}
a.txt: OK
sub/b.txt: OK
status 0
```

Now damage the copy by one byte and check again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf 'x' >> a.txt
md5sum -c checksums.md5; echo "status $?"
cd ..
```

```{.console}
a.txt: FAILED
sub/b.txt: OK
md5sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
status 1
```

The rule from @sec-organizing-projects-raw: make the list on the
**source**, check it on the **receiving** machine, and never recompute
it from the copy (a list made from a damaged copy agrees with the
damage).

**This chapter's check.** Copy the book's raw reads and their checksum
list from your laptop to your cluster folder, and verify them there.
Four steps, all typed on the laptop:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh nova 'mkdir -p /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing/data/raw'
rsync -avn --no-p --no-g ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/ nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing/data/raw/
rsync -av  --no-p --no-g ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/ nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing/data/raw/
ssh nova 'cd /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing/data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5'
```

```{.console}
sending incremental file list
./
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
checksums.md5

sent 167 bytes  received 28 bytes  6.84 bytes/sec
total size is 4,471,546  speedup is 22,931.01 (DRY RUN)
sending incremental file list
./
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
checksums.md5

sent 4,472,921 bytes  received 76 bytes  146,655.64 bytes/sec
total size is 4,471,546  speedup is 1.00
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
```

Make the folder, dry-run, copy, verify on the cluster: two `OK` lines,
the same on Nova, Atlas, and Ceres. On SCINet, use `atlas-dtn` or
`ceres-dtn` (your short names), `/project/<project>/<you>/…`, and
`-avz`.

**What the tools check already.** rsync checks each file it sends
against a checksum of the whole file, so a file damaged on the way is
sent again. But it decides **which** files to send by size and time
alone: a file changed without its size or time changing is skipped
(exercise 2 shows this trap). Globus can verify files after a transfer,
but SCINet's own advice is to switch that off, because "Do NOT verify
file integrity after transfer" "approximately doubles the effective
transfer speed" ([SCINet: Globus](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/data/transfer/globus)).
Either way, `md5sum -c` on the receiving side is the check that does
not depend on any tool's settings.

**What a checksum proves depends on where the list came from.** A list
you made from the source just before copying proves that the copy
matches **that source**; it cannot show damage that was already there
when you made the list. A list from the sequencing facility, from ENA,
or from the original download (your `checksums.md5` from
@sec-organizing-projects-raw) can also catch a file that changed
earlier. That is why the book keeps the original list with the data.
`rsync --checksum` makes rsync compare contents instead of size and
time; it is slower, and it still compares against your source, not
against the original list.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "If the copy finished without an error, the files are fine"
**Reality.** A finished transfer says nothing about a file that was
already wrong at the source or damaged before this copy, and some tools
let you turn their own check off. Check against the original checksum
list, on the receiving machine.
:::

### Moving the project {#sec-working-remotely-move-project}

@sec-organizing-projects ended with three steps for moving a project:
copy the files, reinstall the environment, recreate the links. Now you
have the commands. The reference genome adds a fourth piece, because it
lives **outside** the project (@sec-organizing-projects-shared).

**1. Files.** Make the destination, dry-run, then copy the project
without its environment, results, and logs:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh nova 'mkdir -p /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing'
rsync -avn --no-p --no-g --exclude .pixi --exclude results --exclude logs \
  ~/bioinf-computing/ nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing/
rsync -av  --no-p --no-g --exclude .pixi --exclude results --exclude logs \
  ~/bioinf-computing/ nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing/
ssh nova 'cd /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing/data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5'
```

`.pixi/` stays behind because it is large, built for your laptop's
system, and made of thousands of small files, which count against the
cluster's file limits (@sec-hpc-slurm); step 2 rebuilds it. `results/`
and `logs/` stay behind so that step 4 has to make them again, which is
the point of the test. Your project's `.git/` (@sec-shell-scripts-git)
comes along, so the cluster copy has the same history.
@sec-github shows the usual route for code from then on: push to
GitHub, clone on the cluster. Data still moves with rsync.

**2. Environment.** On the cluster, in the copied project, rebuild the
environment from `pixi.lock`, with pixi and its cache set up as in
@sec-book-setup:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
cd /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing
pixi install --locked
```

On Atlas this took 18 seconds and on Ceres 48. On Nova it took 25 to 40
minutes in November 2026, much longer than the first install, for
reasons the site is looking into. If it is slow for you, let it run, or
run it in an interactive job (@sec-hpc-slurm).

**3. Reference data, then the link.** rsync copies `data/ref` as a link,
not as the files it points to, so on the cluster it points at a laptop
folder that does not exist:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
ls -l data/ref
ls data/ref/
```

```{.console}
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 <netid> <group> 95 Nov 22 21:26 data/ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
ls: cannot access 'data/ref/': No such file or directory
```

The reference needs its own copy. If your lab or site already keeps
this exact reference, you can link to theirs, **after** checking that
its checksums match your `checksums.md5`. Otherwise copy your small
folder through the DTN into a reference area in your own cluster folder,
with the same name as on the laptop (not in your cluster home, which is
small), and check it there:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ssh nova 'mkdir -p /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-shared/references'
rsync -av --no-p --no-g ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test \
  nova-dtn:/work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-shared/references/
ssh nova 'cd /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test && md5sum -c checksums.md5'
```

```{.console}
genome.fa.gz: OK
genes.gtf.gz: OK
```

(No slash on the source this time: you want the folder itself.) Then
replace the link with the rule from @sec-organizing-projects-shared:
look, `unlink` without a trailing slash, link, look again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
cd /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-computing
ls -l data/ref
unlink data/ref
ln -s /work/<group>/<netid>/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test data/ref
ls data/ref/
```

```{.console}
checksums.md5  genes.gtf.gz  genome.fa.gz  README.md
```

Why not just `ln -s` over the old link? It refuses:

```{.console}
ln: failed to create symbolic link 'data/ref': File exists
```

and if the old link had pointed at a folder that does exist, `ln -s`
would quietly have made the new link **inside** that folder instead.

**4. Prove it runs.** Run the pipeline from @sec-shell-scripts-pipeline
on the cluster, check its exit status, and compare its results with the
laptop's:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (login node)"}
pixi run bash src/run_all.sh; echo "run_all status $?"
md5sum results/*.tsv
```

```{.console}
…
run_all status 0
3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
```

Run `md5sum results/*.tsv` in the laptop's project too: the numbers
should be the same, and they were, on Nova and on Atlas. Check the exit
status, not only the files. On one try, the reference copy had failed
without anyone noticing, `02_gtf_summary.sh` stopped with `ERROR:
missing or empty: data/ref/genes.gtf.gz`, and yet an old
`results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv`, copied over from the laptop, still
matched. That is why step 1 leaves `results/` behind. The move is done
when all of these pass: the destination exists, both checksum lists say
`OK`, the new link lists the reference, the environment installed, and
the pipeline exits 0 with the same results.

: What happens to each part of the project in a move. {#tbl-move-project}

| Part | Copy it? | How | Why |
|:-----|:---------|:----|:----|
| scripts, docs, `pixi.toml`, `pixi.lock` | yes | `rsync -av --no-p --no-g` | the project itself |
| `data/raw/` | yes | same, then `md5sum -c` on the cluster | prove the data arrived intact |
| `.pixi/` | no | `pixi install --locked` on the cluster | large, built for one system, many files |
| reference folder (outside the project) | yes, or use a site copy | `rsync` through the DTN, `md5sum -c`; a site copy only if its checksums match | the link points to it |
| `data/ref` link | it arrives broken | `unlink`, then `ln -s` to the cluster copy | it points at a laptop path |
| `.git/` | comes along | (@sec-github: clone instead) | the history |
| `results/`, `logs/` | no | `--exclude`; rerun the pipeline | the cluster run must make its own |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `rsync` finished without errors. Do you still run
`md5sum -c`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Yes. rsync may have skipped a file it judged unchanged by size and time,
and the original checksum list (from the facility or the download) also
catches a file damaged or mixed up before this copy, which a list made
from the source just now cannot. For these files it costs seconds.
:::
:::

## Summary {#sec-working-remotely-summary}

- `ssh host command` runs one command on the cluster and brings back its
  output and exit status. Quotes decide where `$` is expanded. rsync
  uses the same mechanism, so a startup file that prints breaks it:
  `ssh host true | wc -c` must print `0`. Never ignore "REMOTE HOST
  IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED".
- An SSH key is a pair: the public key goes on servers, the private key
  stays on your laptop behind a passphrase, and the agent remembers the
  unlocked key. On Nova a key replaces the code and password (over the
  VPN, to a named login node); SCINet uses its daily `step` certificate.
  Windows' Ubuntu and Windows' own ssh each need their own setup.
- `~/.ssh/config` gives hosts short names and settings; for most options
  the first value found wins, so specific blocks go first and `Host *`
  last. Check every change with `ssh -G`. Connection sharing reuses one
  sign-in per host (not in Windows' own ssh). `ProxyJump` reaches a
  machine through another; @sec-hpc-slurm uses it.
- tmux keeps a shell running on the machine where you started it;
  detach with {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd D >}}, reattach with `tmux
  attach -t name`. A session lives on one login node, so note
  `hostname`. It survives dropped connections, not reboots, and it does
  not make the login node a place for heavy work.
- Copy with rsync from the laptop, to the transfer node. Dry-run first;
  a slash on the source means "the contents of"; make the destination
  with `ssh host 'mkdir -p …'`; into project folders use `-av --no-p
  --no-g`; rerun to finish. Use `scp` for one file and Globus for big
  or many files.
- Prove a copy with `md5sum -c` on the receiving machine, against the
  original list. Move a project in four parts: files (without `.pixi`,
  `results`, `logs`), environment (`pixi install --locked`), reference
  data and a replaced link, and a pipeline run that exits 0 with the
  same results.

@tbl-ch09-commands collects the chapter's commands.

: The chapter's commands on one page. {#tbl-ch09-commands}

| Task | Command |
|:-----|:--------|
| Run one command remotely | `ssh nova hostname`, `ssh nova 'cd dir && ls'` |
| Check for a clean shell | `ssh nova true \| wc -c` (must be `0`) |
| Remove one changed host key | `ssh-keygen -R <host>` (after the site confirms) |
| Make a key | `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "label"` |
| Use the agent | `eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"`, `ssh-add`, `ssh-add -l` |
| Install a key (Nova) | `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub <netid>@nova-login-1.its.iastate.edu` |
| See what ssh will do | `ssh -G nova` |
| Shared connection | `ssh -O check nova`, `ssh -O exit nova` |
| tmux | `tmux new -s name`, {{< kbd Ctrl-B >}} {{< kbd D >}}, `tmux ls`, `tmux attach -t name`, `tmux kill-session -t name` |
| Make a remote folder | `ssh nova 'mkdir -p /path/to/dir'` |
| Copy a folder to a project folder | `rsync -av --no-p --no-g src/ nova-dtn:/path/dir/` (dry run: add `-n`) |
| Copy back to the laptop | `rsync -av nova-dtn:/path/results/ results/` |
| Copy one file | `scp file nova-dtn:/path/` |
| Verify on the receiving side | `ssh nova 'cd /path && md5sum -c checksums.md5'` |
| Replace a link | `ls -l data/ref`, `unlink data/ref`, `ln -s /new/target data/ref`, `ls data/ref/` |

## Exercises {#sec-working-remotely-exercises}

Exercises 1–4 work on the laptop alone (exercise 3 and 4 go further
with a cluster); exercise 5 is the chapter's check on a cluster, with a
laptop version; exercise 6 is optional. Practise in
`~/bioinf-computing-ch09` and record what you did and saw in a
`NOTEBOOK.md` there.

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. The slash and the dry run (laptop).** After
@sec-working-remotely-transfer.

In a new folder, `~/bioinf-computing-ch09/ex1`, make a tree with
`mkdir -p tree/sub && printf '1\n' > tree/one.txt && printf '2\n' >
tree/sub/two.txt`. Before running each command, write down what you
expect `find … | sort` to show: `rsync -a tree t1`, `rsync -a tree/ t2`,
and `rsync -av -n tree/ t3`. Run them and compare. Then add
`tree/three.txt` and show that a second `rsync -av tree/ t2` sends only
the new file.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`t1` holds `t1/tree/one.txt` and `t1/tree/sub/two.txt` (the folder
itself was copied); `t2` holds `t2/one.txt` and `t2/sub/two.txt` (its
contents). The dry run lists `./`, `one.txt`, `sub/`, `sub/two.txt`,
ends with `(DRY RUN)`, and `t3` does not exist afterwards. The second
copy to `t2` lists only `./` and `three.txt`.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Catch a damaged copy, and a stale one (laptop).** After
@sec-working-remotely-move.

In `~/bioinf-computing-ch09/ex2`, make `orig/s.txt` containing `AAAA`,
make a checksum list in `orig/`, and copy with `rsync -a orig/ copy/`.

1. Check the copy with `md5sum -c` inside `copy/`. Append one byte to
   `copy/s.txt`, check again, then repair it with the same rsync and
   check once more.
2. The trap. Change one letter in `orig/s.txt` without changing its size
   or time: `printf 'AAAB\n' > orig/s.txt.new && touch -r orig/s.txt
   orig/s.txt.new && mv orig/s.txt.new orig/s.txt`. Run `rsync -av
   orig/ copy/` and look at `copy/s.txt`. Then run `rsync -av
   --checksum orig/ copy/` and look again.

What does this tell you about rsync's quick check and about `md5sum -c`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
1. `OK`, then `FAILED` with the `WARNING` line and status 1; rsync
   resends the file because its size changed, and the check says `OK`
   again.
2. The plain rsync sends nothing, and `copy/s.txt` still says `AAAA`:
   same size, same time, so rsync's quick check thinks it is unchanged.
   With `--checksum`, rsync compares contents, resends it, and the copy
   says `AAAB`. rsync's quick check looks at size and time; `md5sum -c`
   looks at the bytes. (The list in `orig/` still holds `AAAA`'s
   checksum, so `md5sum -c` now reports `FAILED` in both folders: the
   list describes the file as it was when you made it.)
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. A key and a config (laptop; cluster optional).** After
@sec-working-remotely-config.

Make an ed25519 key with a passphrase (skip this if you already have
one), and load it into the agent (`ssh-add`; on a Mac, the first login
does it). Write config entries for your site's login node and transfer
node with `User` and `ServerAliveInterval`: in your real
`~/.ssh/config` after a dated backup if you have a cluster account,
otherwise in `sample-config`. Prove them with `ssh -G` (add `-F
sample-config` for the practice file).

With a cluster account: on a site that allows keys, install your public
key and record what a login asks now. If you sign in with a code, add
connection sharing and record how many prompts two quick logins give
with and without it, for the login node and for the transfer node
(`ssh -O check` on each). On SCINet, read the file `step` wrote (`cat
~/.step/ssh/config`) and explain each of its lines.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`ssh -G nova-dtn | grep -E '^(hostname|user|serveraliveinterval) '`
should print your user name, the transfer node's full name, and
`serveraliveinterval 60`. On Nova with a key (over the VPN), a login
asks only the key's passphrase, once; with the agent, nothing. With a
code and no sharing, quick logins can ask twice each (a code cannot be
reused); with sharing, the second login to the same host asks nothing,
but the transfer node needs its own first sign-in. On SCINet: `Match
exec` limits the block to SCINet hosts, `User` supplies your name,
`UserKnownHostsFile` holds SCINet's host certificate authority, and
`ProxyCommand` runs `step`, which renews your certificate when needed.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Survive a disconnect (laptop; cluster preferred).** After
@sec-working-remotely-tmux.

Start a tmux session named `ex4`, run `bash ticker.sh` in it, detach,
and close the terminal window (on a cluster: turn your Wi-Fi off for a
minute). Reconnect, find the session, and reattach. Record `hostname`,
the `tmux ls` line, and whether the times have a gap. End the session
with `tmux kill-session -t ex4`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`tmux ls` shows `ex4: 1 windows (created …)`, and after `tmux attach -t
ex4` the ticker's times run on with no gap. On a cluster, if `tmux ls`
finds nothing, check `hostname`: you may be on the other login node; log
in to the node you noted, by name.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 5. Move the project (cluster; the chapter's check).** After
@sec-working-remotely-move.

Move `~/bioinf-computing` to your cluster folder as in
@sec-working-remotely-move-project: make the destination; dry-run, then
copy through the transfer node with `--no-p --no-g`, leaving out
`.pixi/`, `results/`, and `logs/`; verify `data/raw` with `md5sum -c`
on the cluster; copy (or find and check) the reference folder and verify
it; replace `data/ref`; run `pixi install --locked`; run `pixi run bash
src/run_all.sh`, check that it exits 0, and compare `md5sum
results/*.tsv` with your laptop's.

**No cluster?** Do it in a **copy** on the laptop, never your real
project: `rsync -a --exclude .pixi ~/bioinf-computing/
~/bioinf-computing-ch09/fake-cluster/`. Its `data/ref` still points at
your real reference, so it works and hides the problem. Point the copy's
link at a folder that does not exist (`unlink data/ref && ln -s
/no/such/folder data/ref` inside `fake-cluster`), see `ls data/ref/`
fail, then replace it with the right one. Explain which step a laptop
copy cannot really test.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
On the cluster: both `md5sum -c` runs print `OK` for every file, `ls
data/ref/` lists `checksums.md5`, `genes.gtf.gz`, `genome.fa.gz`, and
`README.md`, `run_all.sh` exits 0, and the two `md5sum results/*.tsv`
lines match the laptop's (`3b9c2b4c…` and `e1d81de7…` for the book's
data). On the laptop: `ls data/ref/` fails with `No such file or
directory` while the link points at `/no/such/folder`, and lists the
reference again after you replace it. A laptop copy cannot test the
real problem, a link that points at another machine's file system,
because the laptop's own reference folder is always there.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 6. Globus (optional; SCINet or Nova account).** After
@sec-working-remotely-transfer.

Install Globus Connect Personal on your laptop, and transfer the two
FASTQ files to your site's collection ("SCINet-Ceres", "SCINet-Atlas",
or "Nova DTN"), into a new folder. Check them with `md5sum -c` on the
cluster. Keep the laptop awake, with Globus Connect Personal running,
until the transfer finishes. Record whether file verification was on in
the transfer settings. (SCINet suggests turning it off for speed; for this tiny
transfer, leave it on.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Both files say `OK` when you run `md5sum -c` against the original list
in the new folder (copy `checksums.md5` there too, or point `md5sum -c`
at it). Whether verification was on by default depends on Globus's
current settings page; whatever it was, your `md5sum -c` is the check
that does not depend on it.
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-working-remotely-reading}

- @buffalo2015bioinformatics, *Bioinformatics Data Skills*, chapter 4
  "Working with Remote Machines" and the part of chapter 6 on
  transferring data --- SSH, keys, config files, tmux, `rsync`, and
  checksums, written for the same readers as this chapter.
- @shotts2025linux, *The Linux Command Line*, the networking chapter ---
  `ssh`, `scp`, and `sftp` in a few pages, with more on the network
  tools around them; free online.
- @microsoft2026remotessh, *Remote Development using SSH* --- how VS
  Code's Remote-SSH uses your keys and `~/.ssh/config`, including jump
  hosts, for when you edit on a compute node in @sec-hpc-slurm.
- The OpenSSH manual pages, [`ssh_config(5)`](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config.5)
  and [`ssh(1)`](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh.1) --- every option in
  @tbl-ssh-config-options, exactly; read `ControlPath` for the `%C`
  token and `ProxyJump` for jump hosts.
- The [rsync manual page](https://download.samba.org/pub/rsync/rsync.1),
  section *USAGE* for the trailing-slash rule and *OPTIONS* for `--perms`,
  `--group`, `--partial`, and `--checksum`; and the tmux wiki's
  [*Getting Started*](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Getting-Started)
  for everything beyond @tbl-tmux-keys.
